## Methods

Thin film preparation. High-quality La CoRuO (LCRO) thin films were epitaxially grown on
2 6
SrTiO (STO) and 0.5 wt% Nb-doped SrTiO (Nb-STO) substrates. Films were grown at a
3 3
temperature of 770 ℃ at an oxygen partial pressure of 150 mTorr, where the pulsed laser deposition
was carried out by a KrF excimer laser (248 nm) at a laser fluence of 1.47 J cm-2 and 2 Hz. After
growth, the films were cooled down to room temperature at a rate of 10 ℃/min under an oxygen
pressure of 100 Torr to avoid oxygen vacancies.

Structural characterizations. The crystal structures and surface morphologies of the films were
characterized by high-resolution X-ray diffraction (XRD) with Cu K radiation (λ = 1.5405 Å)
Sα
(Empyrean, PANalytical) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) (MFP-3D origin, Asylum Research
AFM), respectively.

Physical properties characterizations. Macroscopic magnetic measurements were performed
with an MPMS3 SQUID-VSM magnetometer (Quantum Design). All measurements were
performed by applying in-plane magnetic fields. The M-T curves were recorded during the sample
warm-up process after field-cooling at 1 kOe. Transport measurements were measured by a
Quantum Design Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS). Precision Premier II
Ferroelectric Tester (Radiant Technologies) was used to measure P-E hysteresis loops. Pt
electrodes were plated on the films for measurement. Piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM)
measurements were conducted by Asylum Research MFP-3D origin with an HVA 220 high-
voltage amplifier.

SHG measurements. The polarization-dependent SHG measurements were conducted by using a
custom laser-scanning microscope system43, with a Ti:sapphire mode-locking femtosecond laser
(MaiTai SP, Spectra-Physics) serving as the fundamental excitation source (1ω). The laser emitted
35 fs pulses at 800 nm center wavelength, with average power adjustable from 50 to 200 mW.
SHG signals were detected by a photomultiplier tube (PMT) equipped with an optical bandpass
filter to suppress residual 800 nm reflected light. For temperature-dependent SHG studies, an open
heating stage was employed, and as soon as the desired temperature was reached, the temperature
was kept for ~5 minutes before starting the measurement to ensure the accuracy and stability of
the sample temperature. During the entire measurement process, the focal spot position and sample
morphology were verified at each temperature points to ensure consistent incident power and
measurement location.

Scanning transmission electron microscopy. Scanning transmission electron microscopy
investigations, including HAADF-STEM imaging, iDPC-STEM imaging, and EELS
measurements, were performed using an aberration-corrected FEI Titan Cubed Themis G2
microscope operated at 300 kV. The instrument is equipped with an X-FEG electron source, a
monochromator, dual aberration correctors, a Gatan GIF Quantum ER energy filter with
DualEELS capability, and a Super-X EDXS detector system. For HAADF imaging, a collection
angle of 48-200 mrad was used. iDPC-STEM images were acquired using a four-quadrant
segmented DF4 detector under the same accelerating voltage. The EELS spectra were recorded
using DualEELS mode, which allows simultaneous acquisition of low-loss and core-loss spectra.
The zero-loss peak was used to calibrate the energy scale, and plural scattering effects were
corrected accordingly to ensure accurate interpretation of the electronic structure.

X-ray spectroscopic measurements. The X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) measurements
are performed at the I06 beamline of the Diamond Light Source at room temperature in a total
electron yield mode. The spectra of Co L-edge, Ru M-edge and O K-edge are measured by
changing the incident angle of the linearly polarized x-ray beam.

Polarized Neutron Reflectivity Measurement. Polarized neutron reflectivity (PNR)
measurements on a La CoRuO epitaxial film were conducted on the Multipurpose Reflectometer
2 6
(MR) beamline at the Chinese Spallation Neutron Source (CSNS). The sample with a thickness of
about 30-nm La CoRuO thin film was grown on STO (111) substrate with a size of 10 mm by 5
2 6
mm by 0.5 mm. The room temperature neutron reflectivities were measured under an in-plane
magnetic field of 1 T as a function of the wave vector transfer along the film surface normal. R++
and R-- represent the reflectivities from the spin-up and spin-down polarized neutrons, respectively.
PNR data were fitted using GenX software.

Density functional theory calculations. The first-principles calculations are based on density
functional theory (DFT) within the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) utilizing the revised
Perdew-Becke-Erzenhof functional for solids (PBEsol) implemented in the Vienna ab initio
Simulation Package50-53 (VASP). The Co’s 3p63d74s2 and Ru’s 4p64d75s1 were treated as valence
electrons. To describe the correlated 3d electrons of Co and 4d electrons of Ru, the GGA+U
method was adopted54. The U value was tested from 3 to 5 eV for Co and from 2 to 4 eV for Ru
eff
in bulk LCRO, as summarized in Supplementary Fig. 14. Then, U = 4 eV for Co’s 3d orbitals
eff
and U = 2 eV for Ru’s 4d orbitals are adopted, respectively. To initialize the meta-GGA
eff
calculations, wavefunctions and charge densities from pre-converged GGA+U calculations were
employed as a starting point to mitigate convergence difficulties55-56. A cutoff energy of 500 eV is
used for the plane-wave bases, and a Γ-centered 5×5×1 (5×5×5 for LCRO bulk) k-point mesh for
the Brillouin zone integration is adopted for the strained LCRO thin films. A convergence threshold
of 10−6 eV was used for the electronic self-consistency loop. The lattice constants and internal
atomic coordinates were relaxed until the Hellman-Feynman force on each atom is less than 0.005
eV/Å. The ferroelectric polarization was calculated by using the Berry phase method57. And the
amplitudes of the octahedral rotation modes were constrained to specific values, and the positions
of all other ions (La, Co, Ru) were relaxed during these calculations.

### Reviewer 1

The study of Li et al promises room temperature multiferroicity in strained La2CoRuO6, opening routes to low power
spintronic applications. The conclusions are drawn on the basis of advanced experimental techniques as well as density
functional theory calculations. The paper is well written, even though the DFT appears rather disconnected from the
experimental results. It could be added here and there to support experimental results rather than just a final section at the
end of the manuscript.
Although the paper reads quite well and the presented results are sound, I feel a bit frustrated at the end of the manuscript. It
does not deliver what is promised in the title: although the compound is certainly polar, the are no evidence of ferroelectricity.
Showing polar displacements is not sufficient to claim it is ferroelectric (see Nature 533, 68 2016 for a similar study but with
polar metals). In the present manuscript, there are no FE loops (polarization reversal), just hints of polar domains, and DFT
calculations do not provide any quantification of the spontaneous polarization – we only know that Berry phase calculations
have been performed! Furthermore, polar displacements are induced by the symmetry breaking induced by slightly different
octahedra rotations amplitudes between consecutive planes along the growth direction. Nevertheless, as shown on figure
3g, the variation of angles between consecutive planes does not seem to be very large, so I expect that the B cation off
centring to be small, and so might be the spontaneous polarization.
Unless authors can provide significant improvement regarding the FE properties of their compound, I cannot recommend
publication of the present manuscript.
I append below other remarks and suggestions to be considered prior to a resubmission at Nature Communications or
elsewhere:
- I do not understand how the DFT calculations are performed with the varying octahedral rotation amplitudes presented in
Fig. 6.d. It seems that different rotations amplitudes are frozen, but are other atoms allowed to relax in position? If not, the
only polarization that can emerge is an electronic polarization. The method is not discussed in the manuscript even though
this is a key element of the paper.
- Since the B cation displacements might be very small, I expect the polarization to be rather low. Could the authors use DFT
and Born effective charges to estimate locally the polarization in their supercell?
- Furthermore, the polarization being induced by different rotation amplitude between consecutive planes, I expect that the
reversal of the polarization to go through the reversal of tilt patterns. Rotations are known to be associated with very large
energy gains, one to two orders of magnitude larger than polarization in oxides. The reversal of the polarization therefore
appears to be unlikely. Could the authors check this possibility with their DFT by computing the energy barrier for instance?
- DFT results are highly sensitive to the choice of exchange-correlation parameters. Nowadays, parameter free calculations
with meta-GGA are able to capture the correct trend in terms of physical properties of transition metal oxide compounds.
(PRB 111, 144406 2025; PRB 102 145112 2020, PRB 100 035119 2019 for instance). Could the authors benchmark their
results with parameter-free calculations?
- Does DFT predict a checkerboard pattern for the ground state of the compound?
- The gap appears to be rather small (0.55 eV from DFT). Can the author rule out any leakage current preventing the
application of an E-field to reverse the polarization?

### Reviewer 2

In recent years, theoretical and experimental investigations have aimed to achieve a multiferroic state in oxide materials.
However, the lack of materials with significant ferroelectric polarisation, magnetic moment and high critical temperatures
currently prevents the practical application of this state. In their study, the authors investigate La₂CoRuO₆ thin films for this
purpose. The double perovskite (DP) structure can accommodate two magnetic cations, which order in the structure due to
their different ionic sizes. A combination of exchange interactions and epitaxial strain renders the system ferrimagnetic, while
local fluctuations in the rotation angle of the oxygen octahedra give rise to an electric dipole and polar nano-domains. These
claims stem from the authors' analysis of a variety of experimental and theoretical data.
Currently, many of these claims are overstated.
The term 'multiferroism', used in the title, indicates the coexistence of two hysteresis properties; here, these should be
magnetism and ferroelectricity. Currently, there is no indication of a ferroelectric state.
Ab initio calculations performed by the authors indicate the absence of a polar state in coherently strained structures.
The experimental data shown in Figure 3g demonstrate a progressive increase in the oxygen octahedron rotation (OOR) angle,
from 0° in the cubic STO substrate to the bulk value of LCRO. This behaviour is characteristic of an epitaxial thin film, in
which the OORs are coupled across the film/substrate interface, and has been extensively discussed in the literature.
The authors achieve a polar state in their calculations by introducing this progressive increase in the OOR angle (Figure 6d).
However, given the direction of the gradient in the OOR angle, the polarisation has a clearly defined crystallographic
orientation. In contrast, Figure 4c shows that the polar axis orientation in their films aligns with different crystallographic
directions and is therefore unrelated to the previously discussed mechanism. To explain this discrepancy, the authors
introduce 'a gradient suppression of oxygen octahedral rotation (OOR) with inhomogeneous evolution'. Since OORs are
coupled via the sharing of oxygen anions between adjacent octahedra, it is unclear how the system can accommodate such
local distortions on a very short length scale in the absence of a driving mechanism.

### Reviewer 3

The present MS reports an experimental and theoretical study of the onset of ferrimagnetism and local polar order in
epitaxial thin films of the double perovskite La2CoRuO6 grown on [001]- and [111]-oriented Nb-doped SrTiO3 substrates.
The authors find that the in-plane compressive strain leads to enhanced lattice distortions that combine with the high spin
state of Co2+ and an ordered B-site cation arrangement that act to strengthen the Co-O-Ru antiferromagnetic exchange
interaction and to induce a ferrimagnetic state, while the presence of a gradient in the BO6 octahedral rotations is suggested
to drive the onset of polar nanodomains. Overall, I find the experimental work to be well carried out, in particular, by
providing an extended characterization of the system with techniques ranging from x-ray diffraction and absorption
spectroscopy, neutron reflectometry and TEM, supplemented by first principles calculations. As I see it, the key result is the
presentation of a new approach to controlling the exchange coupling in the double perovskites by tuning the B-cation
composition and atomic ordering. However, the main result claimed in the paper, the synthesis of room-temperature
multiferroicity in strained La2CoRuO6 films is not fully demonstrated, since the presence of long-range ferroelectric order,
ferroelectric switching and a coupling between magnetic and ferroelectric order parameters are not established.
I have in addition a number of smaller points of criticism that the authors could consider:
- The strain distribution maps in Fig. 1b show an abrupt change along the [111] direction and non-uniform variations along
the perpendicular direction; the text does not make clear what is the reference point used to plot the data, presumably the
SrTiO3 lattice parameters, this needs to be mentioned explicitly. The authors should also indicate to which portion of the
TEM image the strain field corresponds to. I find it interesting that the authors obtain a similar strain state for the La2CoRuO6
films grown along the [001] and [111] directions (Table S2 and Fig. S4). From symmetry, I would expect different film
distortions, tetragonal for the (001) films and trigonal for the (111). How do the authors explain that the (111) films exhibit a
tetragonal symmetry and how is this seen in the TEM images?
- The values mentioned for the saturation magnetization are in fact the magnetization at the highest field applied. It is clear
from the M-H curves that the magnetization is not saturated. Presumably, the diamagnetic contribution from the substrate
was removed and the question arises as to how the high field slopes shown in Fig.2 were determined (it seems surprisingly
identical for the various temperatures).
- The PNR data suggest a reduced magnetization at the SrTiO3 interface, which would not be surprising (somehow,
correlated with an increase in the nuclear density, which is more surprising). The small magnetic moment corresponds to a
small magnetic density and to a very small difference between the spin up and down reflectivities and to a large scatter in
the data points at high momentum transfer. The question here is what the error bars associated with the magnetic moment
values from PNR and how correlated the interfacial moment is with the nuclear density. I suspect that these parameters are
determined mostly from the data at high momentum transfer and may have very larger error bars associated with them.
- In page 12, the authors discuss the presence of ferrimagnetism as arising from an increase in the Ru-O-Co exchange
interactions, but it is not clear at all what is the link between the exchange coupling and the imbalance between the cation
magnetic moments.
- Concerning the oxygen octahedral rotations, the authors speak of a gradient along the out of plane and in the plane
directions, based on the results presented in Fig.3e-g; in fact, the rotation and bond angle seem to vary in a random manner.
It is difficult to see that the average of the values shown in Fig.3e gives Fig.3g. Looking at the Fig.3g, I would be tempted to
conclude that rotation relation occurs within 5 atomic planes. The variations at outer planes are probably within the scatter
error (which should be provided).
- The authors use SHG to determine the presence of polar order in the system. In fact, the authors state that the SHG signal
gives the IP spontaneous polarization. My understanding is that SHG cannot directly measure spontaneous polarization, it
may simply prove the presence of a break of inversion symmetry in the system. From the TEM data, the authors identify
nanodomains where polar distortions are present. However, the criterion for ferroelectricity is more stringent, and requires
not only that a material is polar, but also that the polarization is switchable by an applied electric field.
- I find the presentation of the DFT results not satisfactory. For example, the authors do not explain what is the difference
between the AFM and FiM configurations in Fig.S14 or how the FiM state is implemented in the calculations. The
introduction of a gradient in the octahedral rotation seems to result in a polar state, however, this situation seems to be far
from the experimental case, where the rotations appear random and where the size of the polar nanodomains do not quite
match with the scale of the gradient suggested by Fig.3g (in fact, I would argue there is no clear gradient in the data shown
here).
In conclusion, I find that the present work is still in a preliminary phase as far as demonstrating multiferroic behavior in the
system studied here.

Firstly, we conducted direct polarization-electric field (P-E) measurements to seek
macroscopic evidence of ferroelectric switching. At room temperature, the narrow
bandgap (~ 0.55 eV) of LCRO films leads to significant leakage currents. Although
cooling to 77 K (Fig. R3a) did partially suppress the leakage current, a well-saturated
square hysteresis loop can still not be obtained. Instead, we observed a
characteristic “leaf-shaped” P-E loop (Fig. R3b). We attribute this behavior to the
following combined factors: (1) Persistent leakage current remains even at low
temperature (i.e., 77 K); (2) The polarization is strongly coupled to oxygen octahedral
rotation (OOR) fluctuations, making its switching inherently difficult; (3) As revealed
by the STEM results, polar domains are highly fragmented into nanoscale regions,
forming a relaxor-ferroelectric-like state that suppresses coordinated long-range
switching.
The observed “leaf-shaped” hysteresis is consistent with a dipole glass state, a
phenomenon reported in a recent study of SrTiO homoepitaxial films, where a similar
3
dipole glass state was induced by local symmetry manipulation (Phys. Rev. Lett. 131,
246801 (2023)). While not constitutive proof on its own, such a characteristic loop
shape has been reported in other emergent ferroelectric systems facing similar
challenges (Nat. Commun. 10, 1409 (2019); Nat. Commun. 16, 6417 (2025)). We
therefore present these data as part of a cumulative body of evidence, while
acknowledging the limitations of the macroscopic measurement.
Secondly, considering the challenges of macroscopic measurement, we turn to
piezoelectric force microscopy (PFM) measurements, providing direct nanoscale
evidence to further illustrate the switching of polarization. As shown in Fig. R4, our
PFM domain switching experiments successfully demonstrate reversible and stable
domain writing and reading. The clear reversal of the PFM phase contrast upon
applying bias pulses of opposite polarities is a definitive proof of ferroelectricity at the
4
micro-scale. This is a widely accepted methodology when P-E loops are inconclusive,
as seen in similar works like room-temperature ferroelectricity in Bi₂O₂Se thin
film (Nano Letters, DOI: 10.1021/acs.nanolett.5c04402) and ferroelectricity in four-
unit-cell freestanding BiFeO
3
film (Nature, 570, 87-90 (2019)).

However, reliably simulating this specific energy barrier within our current DFT
framework is not feasible. The polarization in our system originates from the symmetry
breaking caused by differing oxygen octahedral rotation amplitudes between adjacent
layers. This difference likely stems from either local strain inhomogeneity or the
dissimilar response of various oxygen octahedra to strain, which motivates and couples
multi-mode distortions. In our DFT calculation, the ferroelectric state is constructed by
mimicking the experimental gradient of oxygen octahedral rotation. This ferroelectric
state is higher in energy than the nonpolar state with uniform rotation. Thus, an energy
well will be obtained during the ferroelectric switching simulation, instead of an energy
barrier. Presently, no straightforward DFT approach can accurately capture this specific
barrier within a tractable supercell that fully accounts for the real material environment.
Nevertheless, our experimental PFM measurements demonstrate that polarization
switching does occur at the nanoscale under a sufficiently high local electric field (Fig.
R4, added as Fig. 6a). This suggests that the switching mechanism in our system may

Response: We thank the reviewer for this excellent question. Our DFT-calculated
bandgap of 0.55 eV indeed points to a narrow-gap semiconductor system. This
characteristic does present challenges for applying high electric fields in macroscopic
P-E loop measurements. In addition, our experimental transport data also supports the
small bandgap. The film exhibits a room-temperature resistivity of 1-2 Ω·cm,
confirming its semiconducting nature but indicating limited insulation. This is further
corroborated by low-temperature (77 K) measurements, where a leakage current
density of ~10-5 A/cm2 is observed at a modest field of 10 kV/cm (Fig. R3a, added as
Supplementary Fig. 16a).
The high leakage levels at low temperatures and low fields strongly suggest that
obtaining an ideal square P-E loop is practically impossible at higher application fields.
This is why we encountered the “leaf-shaped” P-E hysteresis loop mentioned in our
manuscript (Fig. R3b, added as Supplementary Fig. 16b).
Crucially, this limitation of macroscopic measurements is why we relied on
piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) measurements to demonstrate polarization
switching. The PFM technique applies a highly localized electric field directly through
a sharp conductive tip, which minimizes the leakage path and allows for the poling and
switching of individual nanoscale domains, even in leaky matrices. Therefore, the clear
and reversible domain switching observed in our PFM experiments provides direct
evidence of field-induced polarization reversal (Fig. R4, added as Fig. 6a), which is
not obscured by the macroscopic leakage current that hinders the P-E measurements.

In direct response to this central issue, we have undertaken substantial efforts to

Firstly, we conducted direct polarization-electric field (P-E) measurements to seek

switching.

2. Ab initio calculations performed by the authors indicate the absence of a polar state
in coherently strained structures. The experimental data shown in Figure 3g
demonstrate a progressive increase in the oxygen octahedron rotation (OOR) angle,
from 0° in the cubic STO substrate to the bulk value of LCRO. This behaviour is
characteristic of an epitaxial thin film, in which the OORs are coupled across the
film/substrate interface, and has been extensively discussed in the literature.
The authors achieve a polar state in their calculations by introducing this progressive
increase in the OOR angle (Figure 6d). However, given the direction of the gradient in
the OOR angle, the polarisation has a clearly defined crystallographic orientation. In
contrast, Figure 4c shows that the polar axis orientation in their films aligns with
different crystallographic directions and is therefore unrelated to the previously
discussed mechanism. To explain this discrepancy, the authors introduce “a gradient
suppression of oxygen octahedral rotation (OOR) with inhomogeneous evolution”.
Since OORs are coupled via the sharing of oxygen anions between adjacent octahedra,
it is unclear how the system can accommodate such local distortions on a very short
length scale in the absence of a driving mechanism.
The data shown in Figures 3e and 3f reveal deviations in angles measured over a
column of many atoms. While these angles appear random in the [110] view, they
should also be random in the perpendicular [-110] direction.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this crucial point regarding the
relationship between our DFT predictions and experimental observations. We fully
agree with the reviewer that the apparent discrepancy between the uniformly oriented
polarization predicted by our idealized DFT model (with a perfectly coherent OOR
gradient) and the multi-directional polar axes observed experimentally requires a
thorough and careful explanation.
The resolution to this apparent contradiction lies in recognizing the inherent structural
complexity of real epitaxial films, which extends beyond the idealized model used in
our DFT calculations. Our experimental characterization clearly demonstrates that the
22
film does not experience perfectly uniform strain, nor does it exhibit a perfectly smooth
OOR gradient. Data from microstructural strain analysis (Fig. 1b) and atomic-scale
octahedral angle mapping (Fig. 3c, e, f) reveal significant local strain variations and an
inhomogeneous evolution of OOR, particularly between CoO and RuO octahedra due
6 6
to their distinct chemical characteristics.
We fully concur with the reviewer’s observation regarding the random angular
deviations shown in Fig. 3e and 3f. These local variations across different
crystallographic directions indeed serve as the “driving mechanism” that disrupts the
ideal long-range OOR coupling. The system naturally accommodates such short-
length-scale distortions through its local energy landscape, which is governed by
varying strain fields and distinct cation chemistry. Consequently, while the global OOR
gradient establishes a background favoring polar order, the local structural
inhomogeneities reshape its expression, causing the polarization to manifest as
fragmented nano-domains with varying orientations rather than as a single uniform
polarization vector.
This realistic scenario is analogous to the physics in [La NiMnO /La CoMnO ]
2 6 2 6 n
superlattices, where multi-mode epitaxial growth creates a complex strain landscape
(Nat. Commun. 15, 5549 (2024); Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 046801 (2025); Small Methods
7, 2201246 (2023)). In such systems, the local strain is affected by the microstructures,
and the response of various oxygen octahedrons to strain is different; thus, the multi-
mode distortions of the oxygen octahedron are motivated and coupled with each other
to produce polarization.

1. The present MS reports an experimental and theoretical study of the onset of
ferrimagnetism and local polar order in epitaxial thin films of the double perovskite
La2CoRuO6 grown on [001]- and [111]-oriented Nb-doped SrTiO3 substrates. The
authors find that the in-plane compressive strain leads to enhanced lattice distortions
that combine with the high spin state of Co2+ and an ordered B-site cation
arrangement that act to strengthen the Co-O-Ru antiferromagnetic exchange
interaction and to induce a ferrimagnetic state, while the presence of a gradient in the
BO6 octahedral rotations is suggested to drive the onset of polar nanodomains. Overall,
I find the experimental work to be well carried out, in particular, by providing an
extended characterization of the system with techniques ranging from x-ray diffraction
and absorption spectroscopy, neutron reflectometry and TEM, supplemented by first
principles calculations. As I see it, the key result is the presentation of a new approach
to controlling the exchange coupling in the double perovskites by tuning the B-cation
composition and atomic ordering. However, the main result claimed in the paper, the
synthesis of room-temperature multiferroicity in strained La2CoRuO6 films is not fully
demonstrated, since the presence of long-range ferroelectric order, ferroelectric
switching and a coupling between magnetic and ferroelectric order parameters are not
established.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for her/his positive assessment of our work,
noting that “the experimental work is well carried out, in particular, by providing an
extended characterization of the system…” and recognizing that “the key result is the
presentation of a new approach to controlling the exchange coupling in the double
perovskites by tuning the B-cation composition and atomic ordering.” We agree with
the reviewer that our initial claim of room-temperature multiferroicity was overstated,
as we did not fully demonstrate long-range ferroelectric order or ferroelectric switching.
In direct response to this central issue, we have undertaken substantial efforts to
strengthen the evidence for ferroelectricity. This includes attempting macroscopic
polarization-electric field (P-E) loop measurements and, most critically, performing
detailed piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) experiments to demonstrate the
reversible switching of polar domains at the nanoscale.
Firstly, we conducted direct polarization-electric field (P-E) measurements to seek
macroscopic evidence of ferroelectric switching. At room temperature, the narrow
bandgap (~ 0.55 eV) of LCRO films leads to significant leakage currents. Although
cooling to 77 K (Fig. R15a) did partially suppress the leakage current, a well-saturated
square hysteresis loop can still not be obtained. Instead, we observed a
characteristic “leaf-shaped” P-E loop (Fig. R15b). We attribute this behavior to the
31
following combined factors: (1) Persistent leakage current remains even at low
temperature (i.e., 77 K); (2) The polarization is strongly coupled to oxygen octahedral
rotation (OOR) fluctuations, making its switching inherently difficult; (3) As revealed
by the STEM results, polar domains are highly fragmented into nanoscale regions,
forming a relaxor-ferroelectric-like state that suppresses coordinated long-range
switching.
Fig. R15 (added as Supplementary Fig. 16) (a) In-plane Leakage current density and
(b) ferroelectric hysteresis loops of LCRO (purple) thin film grown on (111)-oriented
STO (blue) substrate measured at 77 K. The top electrode is platinum with a thickness
of 20 nm.
The observed “leaf-shaped” hysteresis is consistent with a dipole glass state, a
phenomenon reported in a recent study of SrTiO homoepitaxial films, where a similar
3
dipole glass state was induced by local symmetry manipulation (Phys. Rev. Lett. 131,
246801 (2023)). While not constitutive proof on its own, such a characteristic loop
shape has been reported in other emergent ferroelectric systems facing similar
challenges (Nat. Commun. 10, 1409 (2019); Nat. Commun. 16, 6417 (2025)). We
therefore present these data as part of a cumulative body of evidence, while
acknowledging the limitations of the macroscopic measurement.
Secondly, considering the challenges of macroscopic measurement, we turn to
piezoelectric force microscopy (PFM) measurements, providing direct nanoscale
evidence to further illustrate the switching of polarization. As shown in Fig. R16, our
PFM domain switching experiments successfully demonstrate reversible and stable
domain writing and reading. The clear reversal of the PFM phase contrast upon
applying bias pulses of opposite polarities is a definitive proof of ferroelectricity at the
32
micro-scale. This is a widely accepted methodology when P-E loops are inconclusive,
as seen in similar works like room-temperature ferroelectricity in Bi₂O₂Se thin
film (Nano Letters, DOI: 10.1021/acs.nanolett.5c04402) and ferroelectricity in four-
unit-cell freestanding BiFeO
3
film (Nature, 570, 87-90 (2019)).
Fig. R16 (added as Fig. 6a) (a) The schematic diagram of the PFM experimental
measurements. The PFM amplitude and phase images (5×5 μm) of the (111)-oriented
LCRO thin film indicate that the polarization is switchable.
Finally, we employed the Berry phase method to analysis the ferroelectricity. The
polarization intensity calculated by the Berry phase method is approximately (0.288, -
0.257, 0.149) µC/cm2. Noting that this quantitative value depends on the preset
distortion amplitude. Even though, its order of magnitudes is consistent with
experimental observation. The ionic contribution, characterized by the point charge
model, reaches (0.079, -0.487, 0.032) µC/cm2, which is in the same order of magnitude
with the total polarization
In conclusion, we once again sincerely thank the reviewer’s constructive comments,
which guided us to improve our manuscript. Although macroscopic ferroelectric
hysteresis is not ideal, we have provided comprehensive evidence, including PFM
domain switching, SHG, and STEM structural analyses, to strongly demonstrate the
coexistence of switchable polar domains and strong ferrimagnetism at room
temperature.
To more accurately present our findings and avoid overstatement, we have revised the
manuscript’s title to: “Room-temperature ferrimagnetism and polar phase in highly
strained La CoRuO epitaxial films through engineered 3d-4d cation ordering”.

As shown in Fig. R19, in bulk LCRO, which possesses a B-site checkerboard order,
the magnetic order is AFM. In this structure, the nearest-neighbor (NN) interaction is
exclusively the Co-O-Ru super-exchange (J₁), which is antiferromagnetic. This forces
the Co and Ru sublattices to align antiparallel. The next-nearest-neighbor
41
interactions are the Co-O-O-Co (J₂) and Ru-O-O-Ru (J₃) super-exchange, which are
also antiferromagnetic in the bulk, leading to zero net magnetization (Fig. R19).
However, our DFT calculations reveal that the in-plane compressive strain in the thin
film dramatically changes this balance. The in-plane compressive strain in the thin film
modifies the crystal lattice, notably shortening the Co-O-Ru bond lengths. This change
enhances the nearest-neighbor Co-O-Ru super-exchange (J₁), which robustly maintains
the antiparallel alignment between the Co and Ru sublattices. Concurrently, the strain-
induced distortion alters the crystal field and the geometry of the longer-range super-
exchange pathways, specifically the Co-O-O-Co (J₂) and Ru-O-O-Ru (J₃) interactions.
These combined modifications in J₁, J₂, and J₃ under strain make the ferrimagnetic (FiM)
configuration energetically favorable (Fig. R19).
In the stabilized FiM state, the Co2+ (S = 3/2) sublattice aligns ferromagnetically, and
the Ru4+ (S = 1) sublattice also aligns ferromagnetically. These two sublattices are then
locked antiparallel to each other by the strong antiferromagnetic J₁ interaction. The
different magnetic moments of Co2+ (3 ) and Ru4+ (2 ) then yield the net
magnetization (1 ) observed in our strained films. This net magnetization should be

### Reviewer 1

The authors have satisfactorily addressed all the concerns raised in my original report. The manuscript has greatly benefited from the additional experiments and calculations, which demonstrate the existence of switchable polar domains at room temperature, despite the remaining experimental challenges associated with potential leakage currents. This work represents a significant advance in the field of room-temperature multiferroics with strong spin–orbit interactions. I also appreciate the modification of the title, which now more accurately reflects the main findings of the paper. Overall, I find the manuscript to be solid and well supported, and fully deserving of publication in Nature Communications.

### Reviewer 2

Revised Manuscript Commentary
After a thorough examination of the submitted manuscript, I have identified several substantive concerns that remain insufficiently addressed by the authors’ response.
1. Lack of Convincing Experimental Evidence for Ferroelectricity
The original article fails to provide unequivocal experimental proof of a ferroelectric state. In their rebuttal, the authors acknowledge the absence of clear ferroelectric hysteresis loops that would demonstrate a polar, switchable dipole within the films. Instead, they observe a large leakage current.
A particularly misleading element is Figure R3, wherein the authors present a “polarization versus electric field” plot labeled as a ferroelectric hysteresis loop. The I–V trace reveals a complete lack of switching current, indicating that the displayed “polarization” curves are merely the integrated response of a resistive‑capacitive (RC) circuit rather than evidence of ferroelectric switching. Consequently, no ferroelectric signature can be inferred from these data.
2. Interpretation of Piezoresponse Force Microscopy (PFM) Results
Figure R4 displays PFM measurements that the authors claim substantiate ferroelectric switching. However, the data are more consistent with surface charging effects than with genuine ferroelectric domains. Specifically:
• Amplitude Signal: The left‑hand panel shows a pronounced dependence of the PFM amplitude on the applied writing voltage. In a bona fide ferroelectric material, the amplitude of the piezoresponse is largely independent of the writing voltage; only the phase component varies with the polarity of the written domain. The observed amplitude contrast can be attributed to electrostatic charging rather than to a reversal of spontaneous polarization.
Thus, the PFM results do not constitute credible evidence of ferroelectric domain formation or reversible polarization.
3. Discrepancy Between Long‑Range Order Predicted by DFT and Local Structural Disorder
Density-functional theory (DFT) calculations predict a ferroelectric ground state contingent upon a coherent, long‑range gradient in the rotation of oxygen octahedra. Experimentally, however, the films appear to possess substantial local disorder that disrupts the requisite long‑range ordering. While such local distortions may generate isolated dipoles, the random orientation and strong coupling of these dipoles to structural irregularities render collective polarization reversal implausible. The authors’ assertion that their PFM measurements confirm ferroelectric switching of such domains corroborates the suspicious of the feasibility of dipole reversal.
4. Unexplained Low‑Temperature Magnetization Upturn
The magnetization versus temperature curve exhibits an upturn at low temperatures. This feature is not addressed in the authors’ response, leaving its origin ambiguous. Potential contributions—such as impurity phases, magnetic clustering, or spin‑glass behavior—should be investigated and discussed.
Conclusion
Given the unresolved issues outlined above—namely, the absence of definitive ferroelectric hysteresis, the misinterpretation of PFM data, the inconsistency between theoretical predictions and experimental structural disorder, and the unexplained magnetic anomaly—I remain unconvinced that the manuscript meets the standards required for publication in a peer‑reviewed scientific journal. Further experimental validation and comprehensive analysis are necessary before the work can be considered suitable for dissemination.

### Reviewer 3

In this resubmission, the authors address in detail the various issues raised earlier by the reviewers. The most critical aspect, in my opinion, related to the demonstration of ferroelectric order in the system and the claim for multiferroicity. The authors have addressed these aspects, one on the hand by carrying out ferroelectric characterization (P-E switching and PFM), and on the other, by toning down the claims of the original submission. As the authors admit, the P-E loops are rather inconclusive, while the PFM measurements, while suggesting ferroelectric order, could also suffer from artifacts, such as charge deposition, in particular considering the very low estimated ferroelectric polarization. However, the TEM and SHG results do suggest the presence of polar domains, so the evidence points to the presence of ferroelectric order in the system. The revised version is much improved compared to the original, with a better presentation of the first principle results and of the STEM data. Overall, I find the present work to be of high quality and original, highlighting how controlling the cation content and arrangement in the double perovskites can be explored to tune the electronic and functional properties of this class of materials. Hence, I can recommend publication of this MS in Nature Communications.

## Paper

## Abstract

Materials with room-temperature magnetic ordering and switchable polarization are essential for
spintronic devices. Although 3d transition metal oxides exhibit potential, their Curie temperature
(T ) remains unsatisfactory, and coexistence of magnetic and polar order has not been realized in
C
4d/5d oxides. Here, through epitaxial strain and 3d-4d cation ordering engineering, a ferrimagnetic
insulating state (T ~ 623 K) is achieved in La CoRuO films, coexisting with switchable short-
C 2 6
range polar nanodomains. Atomic-scale investigations and density functional theory calculations
reveal that compressive strain enhances lattice distortions. These distortions, combined with high-
spin state of Co2+ ions and ordered BN-site cations, significantly enhance Co-O-Ru
antiferromagnetic superexchange, inducing the ferrimagnetic insulating state. Concurrently, the
gradient BO octahedral rotations with inhomogeneous evolution trigger B-site ions’
6
displacements, driving the formation of polar nanodomains. Our work fills the experimental gap
in realizing magnetic and polar order coexistence in 4d/5d oxides and opens new avenues for
designing high-T multiferroics.

---

## Introduction

Multiferroics, characterized by the coexistence of magnetic and electrically switchable polar
orders with cross-coupling capabilities, hold great promise for next-generation spintronic devices1-
3. Spin-orbit coupling (SOC) is certainly one of the key ‘glues’ that links magnetism and
polarization together4-7. For instance, it mediates the magnetoelectric coupling by translating
symmetry-breaking into charge dipoles or controlling magnetic textures under broken space
inversion symmetry6. Strong SOC is generally essential for enhancing the spin response to electric
stimuli in multiferroics8,9, thereby facilitating ultra-low power consumption, high speed, and high
density in spintronic devices10. However, the strength of SOC is proportional to the atomic number,
therefore it is naturally weak for 3d transition metals. Incorporating heavy elements, such as 4d or
5d transition metals, offers a promising route to enhance the effective SOC. Nevertheless,
experimental studies on the coexistence of magnetic and polar orders in transition metal oxides
containing these heavy elements have never been explored (Supplementary Table S1).

Double perovskite (DP) A BB'O oxides provide enhanced structural flexibility compared to
2 6
simple perovskites11-12. The presence of two distinct transition metal elements at the B/B' sites
offers additional degrees of freedom, creating an ideal platform for designing innovative
multiferroics and exploring the underlying multiferroic coupling behaviors13-15. Crucially, the spin
state associated with the B' site electronic configuration can be profoundly modified by SOC,
particularly when B' ions belong to the 4d or 5d series. Many members in this family exhibit high
magnetic ordering temperatures16-18. A notable example is Sr CrOsO , a ferrimagnetic (FiM)
2 6
insulator with ultra-high Curie temperature16 (T ~ 725 K). Achieving ferroelectricity in such high-
C
T DP materials would represent a significant technological breakthrough. Interestingly, recent
C
theoretical calculations19,20 predicted that the 3d-5d DP Zn FeOsO could be a room-temperature
2 6
(RT) multiferroic, exhibiting a large ferroelectric polarization and FiM ordering. In addition, this
compound is predicted to exhibit strong magnetoelectric coupling, primarily due to the enhanced
SOC effect of the 5d-Os element19. These findings highlight 3d-4d/5d DP oxides as a highly
promising class of materials for exploring new multiferroics.

In this regard, La CoRuO (LCRO) is particularly fascinating because its intrinsic high degree of
2 6
B-site cation ordering enables a pristine and well-organized Co-O-Ru interaction network, while
the 4d Ru ion simultaneously delivers strong SOC21,22. In the bulk form, LCRO crystallizes in a
monoclinic distorted perovskite structure (P2 /n; a = 5.572Å, b = 5.628 Å, c = 7.884 Å, and β =
1
89.99°), and exhibits an antiferromagnetic (AFM) insulating behavior21. It is well known that the
spin states of B/B'-site ions have crucial implications for DP materials' electrical and magnetic
ground states13,16,17,19,20. Cobalt oxides, in particular, have attracted significant attention because
the Co ion can accommodate various spin states and are highly responsive to external stimuli23-25.
It is worth noting that in LCRO, there exists a stable high-spin (HS) state of Co2+ (𝑡5 𝑒2, S = 3/2).
2𝑔 𝑔
Previous studies have demonstrated that HS Co2+ ions show a remarkable ability to regulate
magnetoelectric ground states26-28. For example, vacuum annealing of compressively strained
LaCoO epitaxial film can yield a LaCoO brownmillerite phase with zigzag-ordered oxygen
3 2.5
vacancies, exhibiting ferromagnetic insulating (FMI) behavior with T up to ~ 284 K due to the
C
exotic HS Co2+ state26. Additionally, the FMI state and anomalous Hall effect emerge in
La CoO epitaxial films supported by the HS Co²⁺ state27. Our previous work also demonstrated
2 4±x
that HS Co2+ ions resulting from oxygen vacancies play a significant role in stabilizing a robust
FMI state in tensile-strained LaCoO epitaxial films28.

Although the LCRO bulk has been extensively studied, its epitaxial film growth has not been
reported yet. Lattice distortions in strained films can strongly modify the orbital occupancy of
cations, the strength of superexchange coupling, and related interactions, often leading to
unexpected magnetoelectric properties28-31. Herein, we successfully realize the coexistence of an
RT FiM insulating state (T ~ 623 K) and switchable polar nanodomains in highly B-site cation
C
ordered LCRO epitaxial films. Combined scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM)
investigations and density functional theory (DFT) calculations attribute this emergent coexistence
of magnetic and polar orders to the shrinkage of lattice volume and the gradient suppression of
oxygen octahedral rotations (OOR) with inhomogeneous evolution. Lattice volume reduction
enhances the magnetic interactions along the nearest-neighbor Co-O-Ru path while weakening the
next-nearest-neighbor coupling, leading to the emergence of the FiM insulating state.
Simultaneously, the origin of switchable short-range polar nanodomains is attributed to the
gradient rotations of BO octahedra, which trigger B-site cation displacement and promotes a
6
structural transition from the centrosymmetric non-polar P2 /n phase to the polar 4mm or P2
1 1
phase via the breaking of the sliding surface n. These structural and electronic features are further
corroborated by our first-principles calculations. This work provides the evidence of coexisting
RT magnetic and switchable polar orders in a 4d-oxide, which establishes a prerequisite for
achieving multiferroicity in 3d-4d/5d double perovskites, thereby providing a new platform for
discovering emerging multiferroic materials.

---

## Results

Highly ordered B-site cations in strained LCRO epitaxial films
The DP LCRO films with thickness of approximate 30 nm grown on (111)-and (001)-oriented
SrTiO (STO) substrate were fabricated by pulsed laser deposition (PLD). Typical out-of-plane X-
3
ray diffraction (XRD) θ-2θ scans indicate the epitaxial growth and high phase purity of the films
(Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. 1a, b). The (111) reflection peaks were distinctly observed,
indicating the formation of the checkerboard type B-site ordered DP phase with Co and Ru ions
arranged alternately along the [111] direction. The rocking curve and oscillating peaks of X-ray
reflectivity (XRR) verify the high crystallinity and uniform chemical compositions of the films
(Supplementary Fig. 1c, d and Supplementary Fig. 2). Ex-situ atomic force microscopy (AFM)
images further confirm that all LCRO films have atomically smooth surface (Supplementary Fig.
1a, b). Additionally, to further examine the texture, the in-plane crystalline information of LCRO
films was analyzed by phi-scans of the (101) plane. The threefold symmetry for the (111)-oriented
film and fourfold symmetry for the (001)-oriented film reveal perfect in-plane orientation registry,
indicating a “cube-on-cube” growth mode and single-crystal properties (Supplementary Fig. 3a,
b). This observation was further verified by the high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) STEM
images acquired along the [110] zone axis of the LCRO films (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Fig. 6a,
b). The HAADF-STEM images also show that the LCRO films exhibit high-quality epitaxy and
sharp interfaces with the substrates. Besides, to determine the lattice strain of the films, reciprocal
space mappings (RSMs) were measured and are displayed in Supplementary Fig. 4a, b. The RSMs
suggest that LCRO epitaxial films are coherently strained to the substrates with negligible strain
relaxation. Therefore, based on XRD θ-2θ and RSMs results, the structural parameters of the
LCRO films were determined, including lattice parameters (monoclinic symmetry) a, b, c,
mismatch strain (ε), and lattice volume (Supplementary Table S2). Compared to the LCRO bulk21,
the lattice volumes in these films are effectively reduced. To further confirm the strain exerted by
the substrate on the film, the geometric phase analysis31 (GPA) was performed based on the STEM
images, showing the strain distribution at the interface with nanometer-scale spatial resolution (Fig.
1b). The corresponding in-plane (IP, ε ) and out-of-plane (OP, ε ) strain distribution maps suggest
xx yy
that the IP compressive strain and OP tensile strain within the film are consistent. The mean square
root values of the strain are also consistent with those derived from RSMs.

The fascinating physical properties of DPE materials are closely related to the degree of B-site cation
ordering32-34. To investigate the degree of B-site cation ordering in the LCRO epitaxial films,
aberration-corrected HAADF-STEM28,31,33 imaging was employed. Figure 1c presents a projected
structure and HAADT-STEM image of LCRO along the [110] zone axis. In the projected structure,
Co and Ru ions alternate in columns along the [110] direction, and this pattern is repeated in every
other column along the [001] direction. The corresponding fast Fourier transform (FFT) pattern in
the inset reveals distinct satellite reflections (highlighted by the circles), which are indicative of

Investigation of an unexpected polar phase with nanodomains
The OOR may create polar structure due to strong lattice-charge coupling13,14,15. The macroscopic
polarization of the LCRO film was initially characterized by polarization-electric field (P-E) loop
measurements. A characteristic “leaf-shaped” P-E hysteresis observed at low temperature
(Supplementary Fig. 16b) could be consistent with a polar response. However, its non-ideal shape
likely results from polar nanodomain (or dipole glass state48) and significant persistent leakage, as
evidenced by the accompanying current-voltage characteristics (Supplementary Fig. 16a).
Therefore, this macroscopic measurement alone cannot serve as conclusive evidence for polar
switching. To overcome the limitations of macroscopic measurements and directly probe the polar
behavior at the nanoscale, we further performed detailed piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM)
investigations at room temperature14. We observed a clear butterfly loop and a corresponding phase
hysteresis loop (Supplementary Fig. 17), which confirms the switchable of the polarization.
Subsequently, our PFM domain switching experiments further successfully demonstrated
reversible and stable domain writing and erasing. Clear reversal of the PFM phase contrast upon
applying bias voltages of opposite polarities through the conductive tip confirms that the
spontaneous polarization can be reliably switched by an external electric field (Fig. 6a). To further
investigate the macroscopic polar order and crystal symmetry, we employed optical second-
harmonic generation (SHG) measurements36,49. As schematically illustrated in Fig. 6c, the
rotational anisotropy of the SHG response was characterized using a normal-incidence
configuration. Detailed SHG measurements were conducted across a temperature range of 300 to
500 K (Supplementary Fig. 18). The SHG polarimetry displayed a characteristic double-lobe
structure for measurements in both the horizontal (σ = 0°) and vertical (σ = 90°) polarization
directions, which are parallel and perpendicular to the [110] direction of the sample, respectively
(Fig. 6b and Supplementary Fig. 18). Furthermore, the intensity of SHG response exhibited
remarkable thermal stability, indicating that the proportion of polar domains does not decrease
with increasing temperature (Fig. 6c). Quantitative fitting of the SHG data further confirmed a
distinct domain configuration comprising mixed a₁/a₂ phases, oriented at approximately 45°
relative to the [110] zone axis (Supplementary note 1). The results of fitting indicate that the space
group structure of LCRO has changed from the non-polar centrosymmetric P2 /n in bulk form to
1
the polar 4mm or P2 phase in these epitaxial films through the breaking of the sliding surface n14.
1
The microscopic origin of polar nanodomains in LCRO films were further confirmed through
atomic-scale quantitative analysis using aberration-corrected STEM37. Figure 6d displays a
representative HAADF-STEM image taken from the interior of the LCRO film, where atomic
positions of La and Co/Ru are identified. To evaluate the local polarization, we quantified the
displacement of B-site cations (Co/Ru) relative to the centroid of their surrounding four nearest A-
site (La) cations (Fig. 6d and Supplementary Fig. 19). These displacements define the magnitude
and direction of the polarization vector at the unit-cell level. These calculated displacement vectors
are overlaid on the HAADF-STEM image, with arrow length and color corresponding to the
polarization and magnitude orientation, respectively. To correlated polarization with structural
distortions, we mapped the local c/a ratio, as shown in Fig. 6e, and statistically analyzed the
distribution of polarization angles in Fig. 6f. The polarization vector maps reveal a distribution of
nanoscale polar regions of varying sizes and orientations, consistent with nanoscale structural
variations, as evidenced in the c/a ratio mapping shown in Fig. 6e. Despite the apparent spatial
disorder, the polarization vectors within these polarized domains show a strong preferential
alignment along the [2-20] direction, as confirmed by the predominant angular distribution
between 0° and 15° in Fig. 6f. Within these nanoregions, distinct polar displacements of Co/Ru
atoms (δz ≈ 0.17 Å) are evident, as illustrated in Fig. 6g. Together, these results provide
𝐶𝑜/𝑅𝑢
direct atomic-scale evidence of local polar distortions and demonstrate the existence of nanoscale
polarization disorder within the LCRO films. The collective evidence from the atomically resolved
polar distortions and the macroscopic "leaf-shaped" P-E hysteresis loop consistently points to the
formation of a dipole glass or relaxor-like ferroelectric state in the LCRO films48, where nanoscale
polarization fragmentation suppresses long-range ferroelectric order while permitting local
switchability.

To further understand the origin of polar nanodomains, we performed the Berry phase calculations
to estimate the macroscopic polarization. However, for the ideally strained films, the net
polarization is zero. This is not surprise because its point space group of P2 /n is nonpolar. In other
1
words, a uniform strain can not lead to the polarity observed in experiment. In fact, accompanying
the microscale non-uniform strain, the gradient of OOR with inhomogeneous evolution can be
responsible for the polarity, which induces the displacements of Co/Ru ions with differing
magnitudes and directions (Fig. 6d). To confirm this assumption, we introduced the gradient of
OOR in our DFT structure, by slightly changing the rotation angles of half oxygen octahedra. Then
the output macroscopic polarization becomes nonzero. The Berry phase calculation of a model
structure with proper oxygen octahedral rotations gradient yields a locally polarization of
approximately (0.288, -0.257, 0.149) µC/cm ². The inhomogeneous distortive forces on each ions
are shown in Fig. 6h. This DFT model captures the essential polar mechanism whereby a spatially
varying pattern of oxygen octahedral rotations breaks inversion symmetry. The nanoscale domain
fragmentation observe experimentally arises from intrinsic structural complexities that extend
beyond the idealized model, including local strain variations and the distinct multi-mode
distortions of CoO and RuO octahedra (Fig. 6a-d). The system shows features analogous to a
6 6
hybrid improper ferroelectric, in which the polar state arises from structural distortions13-15.

In summary, by synergistically utilizing subtle strain engineering and B-site cation ordering, we
have achieved a room-temperature coexistence of FiM insulating state and polar nanodomains,
indicating ferroelectric ordering in DP LCRO epitaxial films. The B-site cation ordering in the
films is robust and independent of crystal orientation. Moreover, strain promotes significant lattice
distortions, including the shrinkage of lattice volume and long-range suppression of OOR.
Combining atomic-scale quantitative electron microscopy analysis with DFT calculations, we
unravel the origin of this FiM insulating behavior in which the cooperation of the shrinkage of
lattice volume and HS state of Co2+ contributes to the enhanced strength of the Co-O-Ru
superexchange interaction. The inconsistent response of BO₆ octahedra to strain leads to gradient
OOR with inhomogeneous evolution, driving the formation of switchable polar nanodomains with
a mixed a /a configuration. Insights from this study may point to effective strategies for designing
1 2
materials with coexisting magnetic and polar orders at high temperature. The material we
developed can serve as a starting point to explore a promising platform for multiferroics with
strong magnetoelectric coupling through further engineering.

## Methods

Thin film preparation. High-quality La CoRuO (LCRO) thin films were epitaxially grown on
2 6
SrTiO (STO) and 0.5 wt% Nb-doped SrTiO (Nb-STO) substrates. Films were grown at a
3 3
temperature of 770 ℃ at an oxygen partial pressure of 150 mTorr, where the pulsed laser deposition
was carried out by a KrF excimer laser (248 nm) at a laser fluence of 1.47 J cm-2 and 2 Hz. After
growth, the films were cooled down to room temperature at a rate of 10 ℃/min under an oxygen
pressure of 100 Torr to avoid oxygen vacancies.

Structural characterizations. The crystal structures and surface morphologies of the films were
characterized by high-resolution X-ray diffraction (XRD) with Cu K radiation (λ = 1.5405 Å)
Sα
(Empyrean, PANalytical) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) (MFP-3D origin, Asylum Research
AFM), respectively.

Physical properties characterizations. Macroscopic magnetic measurements were performed
with an MPMS3 SQUID-VSM magnetometer (Quantum Design). All measurements were
performed by applying in-plane magnetic fields. The M-T curves were recorded during the sample
warm-up process after field-cooling at 1 kOe. Transport measurements were measured by a
Quantum Design Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS). Precision Premier II
Ferroelectric Tester (Radiant Technologies) was used to measure P-E hysteresis loops. Pt
electrodes were plated on the films for measurement. Piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM)
measurements were conducted by Asylum Research MFP-3D origin with an HVA 220 high-
voltage amplifier.

SHG measurements. The polarization-dependent SHG measurements were conducted by using a
custom laser-scanning microscope system43, with a Ti:sapphire mode-locking femtosecond laser
(MaiTai SP, Spectra-Physics) serving as the fundamental excitation source (1ω). The laser emitted
35 fs pulses at 800 nm center wavelength, with average power adjustable from 50 to 200 mW.
SHG signals were detected by a photomultiplier tube (PMT) equipped with an optical bandpass
filter to suppress residual 800 nm reflected light. For temperature-dependent SHG studies, an open
heating stage was employed, and as soon as the desired temperature was reached, the temperature
was kept for ~5 minutes before starting the measurement to ensure the accuracy and stability of
the sample temperature. During the entire measurement process, the focal spot position and sample
morphology were verified at each temperature points to ensure consistent incident power and
measurement location.

Scanning transmission electron microscopy. Scanning transmission electron microscopy
investigations, including HAADF-STEM imaging, iDPC-STEM imaging, and EELS
measurements, were performed using an aberration-corrected FEI Titan Cubed Themis G2
microscope operated at 300 kV. The instrument is equipped with an X-FEG electron source, a
monochromator, dual aberration correctors, a Gatan GIF Quantum ER energy filter with
DualEELS capability, and a Super-X EDXS detector system. For HAADF imaging, a collection
angle of 48-200 mrad was used. iDPC-STEM images were acquired using a four-quadrant
segmented DF4 detector under the same accelerating voltage. The EELS spectra were recorded
using DualEELS mode, which allows simultaneous acquisition of low-loss and core-loss spectra.
The zero-loss peak was used to calibrate the energy scale, and plural scattering effects were
corrected accordingly to ensure accurate interpretation of the electronic structure.

X-ray spectroscopic measurements. The X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) measurements
are performed at the I06 beamline of the Diamond Light Source at room temperature in a total
electron yield mode. The spectra of Co L-edge, Ru M-edge and O K-edge are measured by
changing the incident angle of the linearly polarized x-ray beam.

Polarized Neutron Reflectivity Measurement. Polarized neutron reflectivity (PNR)
measurements on a La CoRuO epitaxial film were conducted on the Multipurpose Reflectometer
2 6
(MR) beamline at the Chinese Spallation Neutron Source (CSNS). The sample with a thickness of
about 30-nm La CoRuO thin film was grown on STO (111) substrate with a size of 10 mm by 5
2 6
mm by 0.5 mm. The room temperature neutron reflectivities were measured under an in-plane
magnetic field of 1 T as a function of the wave vector transfer along the film surface normal. R++
and R-- represent the reflectivities from the spin-up and spin-down polarized neutrons, respectively.
PNR data were fitted using GenX software.

Density functional theory calculations. The first-principles calculations are based on density
functional theory (DFT) within the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) utilizing the revised
Perdew-Becke-Erzenhof functional for solids (PBEsol) implemented in the Vienna ab initio
Simulation Package50-53 (VASP). The Co’s 3p63d74s2 and Ru’s 4p64d75s1 were treated as valence
electrons. To describe the correlated 3d electrons of Co and 4d electrons of Ru, the GGA+U
method was adopted54. The U value was tested from 3 to 5 eV for Co and from 2 to 4 eV for Ru
eff
in bulk LCRO, as summarized in Supplementary Fig. 14. Then, U = 4 eV for Co’s 3d orbitals
eff
and U = 2 eV for Ru’s 4d orbitals are adopted, respectively. To initialize the meta-GGA
eff
calculations, wavefunctions and charge densities from pre-converged GGA+U calculations were
employed as a starting point to mitigate convergence difficulties55-56. A cutoff energy of 500 eV is
used for the plane-wave bases, and a Γ-centered 5×5×1 (5×5×5 for LCRO bulk) k-point mesh for
the Brillouin zone integration is adopted for the strained LCRO thin films. A convergence threshold
of 10−6 eV was used for the electronic self-consistency loop. The lattice constants and internal
atomic coordinates were relaxed until the Hellman-Feynman force on each atom is less than 0.005
eV/Å. The ferroelectric polarization was calculated by using the Berry phase method57. And the
amplitudes of the octahedral rotation modes were constrained to specific values, and the positions
of all other ions (La, Co, Ru) were relaxed during these calculations.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The study of Li et al promises room temperature multiferroicity in strained La2CoRuO6, opening routes to low power
spintronic applications. The conclusions are drawn on the basis of advanced experimental techniques as well as density
functional theory calculations. The paper is well written, even though the DFT appears rather disconnected from the
experimental results. It could be added here and there to support experimental results rather than just a final section at the
end of the manuscript.
Although the paper reads quite well and the presented results are sound, I feel a bit frustrated at the end of the manuscript. It
does not deliver what is promised in the title: although the compound is certainly polar, the are no evidence of ferroelectricity.
Showing polar displacements is not sufficient to claim it is ferroelectric (see Nature 533, 68 2016 for a similar study but with
polar metals). In the present manuscript, there are no FE loops (polarization reversal), just hints of polar domains, and DFT
calculations do not provide any quantification of the spontaneous polarization – we only know that Berry phase calculations
have been performed! Furthermore, polar displacements are induced by the symmetry breaking induced by slightly different
octahedra rotations amplitudes between consecutive planes along the growth direction. Nevertheless, as shown on figure
3g, the variation of angles between consecutive planes does not seem to be very large, so I expect that the B cation off
centring to be small, and so might be the spontaneous polarization.
Unless authors can provide significant improvement regarding the FE properties of their compound, I cannot recommend
publication of the present manuscript.
I append below other remarks and suggestions to be considered prior to a resubmission at Nature Communications or
elsewhere:
- I do not understand how the DFT calculations are performed with the varying octahedral rotation amplitudes presented in
Fig. 6.d. It seems that different rotations amplitudes are frozen, but are other atoms allowed to relax in position? If not, the
only polarization that can emerge is an electronic polarization. The method is not discussed in the manuscript even though
this is a key element of the paper.
- Since the B cation displacements might be very small, I expect the polarization to be rather low. Could the authors use DFT
and Born effective charges to estimate locally the polarization in their supercell?
- Furthermore, the polarization being induced by different rotation amplitude between consecutive planes, I expect that the
reversal of the polarization to go through the reversal of tilt patterns. Rotations are known to be associated with very large
energy gains, one to two orders of magnitude larger than polarization in oxides. The reversal of the polarization therefore
appears to be unlikely. Could the authors check this possibility with their DFT by computing the energy barrier for instance?
- DFT results are highly sensitive to the choice of exchange-correlation parameters. Nowadays, parameter free calculations
with meta-GGA are able to capture the correct trend in terms of physical properties of transition metal oxide compounds.
(PRB 111, 144406 2025; PRB 102 145112 2020, PRB 100 035119 2019 for instance). Could the authors benchmark their
results with parameter-free calculations?
- Does DFT predict a checkerboard pattern for the ground state of the compound?
- The gap appears to be rather small (0.55 eV from DFT). Can the author rule out any leakage current preventing the
application of an E-field to reverse the polarization?

### Reviewer 2

In recent years, theoretical and experimental investigations have aimed to achieve a multiferroic state in oxide materials.
However, the lack of materials with significant ferroelectric polarisation, magnetic moment and high critical temperatures
currently prevents the practical application of this state. In their study, the authors investigate La₂CoRuO₆ thin films for this
purpose. The double perovskite (DP) structure can accommodate two magnetic cations, which order in the structure due to
their different ionic sizes. A combination of exchange interactions and epitaxial strain renders the system ferrimagnetic, while
local fluctuations in the rotation angle of the oxygen octahedra give rise to an electric dipole and polar nano-domains. These
claims stem from the authors' analysis of a variety of experimental and theoretical data.
Currently, many of these claims are overstated.
The term 'multiferroism', used in the title, indicates the coexistence of two hysteresis properties; here, these should be
magnetism and ferroelectricity. Currently, there is no indication of a ferroelectric state.
Ab initio calculations performed by the authors indicate the absence of a polar state in coherently strained structures.
The experimental data shown in Figure 3g demonstrate a progressive increase in the oxygen octahedron rotation (OOR) angle,
from 0° in the cubic STO substrate to the bulk value of LCRO. This behaviour is characteristic of an epitaxial thin film, in
which the OORs are coupled across the film/substrate interface, and has been extensively discussed in the literature.
The authors achieve a polar state in their calculations by introducing this progressive increase in the OOR angle (Figure 6d).
However, given the direction of the gradient in the OOR angle, the polarisation has a clearly defined crystallographic
orientation. In contrast, Figure 4c shows that the polar axis orientation in their films aligns with different crystallographic
directions and is therefore unrelated to the previously discussed mechanism. To explain this discrepancy, the authors
introduce 'a gradient suppression of oxygen octahedral rotation (OOR) with inhomogeneous evolution'. Since OORs are
coupled via the sharing of oxygen anions between adjacent octahedra, it is unclear how the system can accommodate such
local distortions on a very short length scale in the absence of a driving mechanism.
The data shown in Figures 3e and 3f reveal deviations in angles measured over a column of many atoms. While these
angles appear random in the [110] view, they should also be random in the perpendicular [-110] direction.
It should also be noted that if the polarization is coupled to local OOR fluctuations, it may be difficult to switch the
polarization orientation.
In any case, these polar nano-domains do not constitute evidence of a ferroelectric state.

resemble the characteristic dependence observed in other ferromagnets or ferrimagnets (see, for instance, Ref. 39). The
authors do not explain the origin of this difference.

### Reviewer 3

The present MS reports an experimental and theoretical study of the onset of ferrimagnetism and local polar order in
epitaxial thin films of the double perovskite La2CoRuO6 grown on [001]- and [111]-oriented Nb-doped SrTiO3 substrates.
The authors find that the in-plane compressive strain leads to enhanced lattice distortions that combine with the high spin
state of Co2+ and an ordered B-site cation arrangement that act to strengthen the Co-O-Ru antiferromagnetic exchange
interaction and to induce a ferrimagnetic state, while the presence of a gradient in the BO6 octahedral rotations is suggested
to drive the onset of polar nanodomains. Overall, I find the experimental work to be well carried out, in particular, by
providing an extended characterization of the system with techniques ranging from x-ray diffraction and absorption
spectroscopy, neutron reflectometry and TEM, supplemented by first principles calculations. As I see it, the key result is the
presentation of a new approach to controlling the exchange coupling in the double perovskites by tuning the B-cation
composition and atomic ordering. However, the main result claimed in the paper, the synthesis of room-temperature
multiferroicity in strained La2CoRuO6 films is not fully demonstrated, since the presence of long-range ferroelectric order,
ferroelectric switching and a coupling between magnetic and ferroelectric order parameters are not established.
I have in addition a number of smaller points of criticism that the authors could consider:
- The strain distribution maps in Fig. 1b show an abrupt change along the [111] direction and non-uniform variations along
the perpendicular direction; the text does not make clear what is the reference point used to plot the data, presumably the
SrTiO3 lattice parameters, this needs to be mentioned explicitly. The authors should also indicate to which portion of the
TEM image the strain field corresponds to. I find it interesting that the authors obtain a similar strain state for the La2CoRuO6
films grown along the [001] and [111] directions (Table S2 and Fig. S4). From symmetry, I would expect different film
distortions, tetragonal for the (001) films and trigonal for the (111). How do the authors explain that the (111) films exhibit a
tetragonal symmetry and how is this seen in the TEM images?
- The values mentioned for the saturation magnetization are in fact the magnetization at the highest field applied. It is clear
from the M-H curves that the magnetization is not saturated. Presumably, the diamagnetic contribution from the substrate
was removed and the question arises as to how the high field slopes shown in Fig.2 were determined (it seems surprisingly
identical for the various temperatures).
- The PNR data suggest a reduced magnetization at the SrTiO3 interface, which would not be surprising (somehow,
correlated with an increase in the nuclear density, which is more surprising). The small magnetic moment corresponds to a
small magnetic density and to a very small difference between the spin up and down reflectivities and to a large scatter in
the data points at high momentum transfer. The question here is what the error bars associated with the magnetic moment
values from PNR and how correlated the interfacial moment is with the nuclear density. I suspect that these parameters are
determined mostly from the data at high momentum transfer and may have very larger error bars associated with them.
- In page 12, the authors discuss the presence of ferrimagnetism as arising from an increase in the Ru-O-Co exchange
interactions, but it is not clear at all what is the link between the exchange coupling and the imbalance between the cation
magnetic moments.
- Concerning the oxygen octahedral rotations, the authors speak of a gradient along the out of plane and in the plane
directions, based on the results presented in Fig.3e-g; in fact, the rotation and bond angle seem to vary in a random manner.
It is difficult to see that the average of the values shown in Fig.3e gives Fig.3g. Looking at the Fig.3g, I would be tempted to
conclude that rotation relation occurs within 5 atomic planes. The variations at outer planes are probably within the scatter
error (which should be provided).
- The authors use SHG to determine the presence of polar order in the system. In fact, the authors state that the SHG signal
gives the IP spontaneous polarization. My understanding is that SHG cannot directly measure spontaneous polarization, it
may simply prove the presence of a break of inversion symmetry in the system. From the TEM data, the authors identify
nanodomains where polar distortions are present. However, the criterion for ferroelectricity is more stringent, and requires
not only that a material is polar, but also that the polarization is switchable by an applied electric field.
- I find the presentation of the DFT results not satisfactory. For example, the authors do not explain what is the difference
between the AFM and FiM configurations in Fig.S14 or how the FiM state is implemented in the calculations. The
introduction of a gradient in the octahedral rotation seems to result in a polar state, however, this situation seems to be far
from the experimental case, where the rotations appear random and where the size of the polar nanodomains do not quite
match with the scale of the gradient suggested by Fig.3g (in fact, I would argue there is no clear gradient in the data shown
here).
In conclusion, I find that the present work is still in a preliminary phase as far as demonstrating multiferroic behavior in the
system studied here.

Firstly, we conducted direct polarization-electric field (P-E) measurements to seek
macroscopic evidence of ferroelectric switching. At room temperature, the narrow
bandgap (~ 0.55 eV) of LCRO films leads to significant leakage currents. Although
cooling to 77 K (Fig. R3a) did partially suppress the leakage current, a well-saturated
square hysteresis loop can still not be obtained. Instead, we observed a
characteristic “leaf-shaped” P-E loop (Fig. R3b). We attribute this behavior to the
following combined factors: (1) Persistent leakage current remains even at low
temperature (i.e., 77 K); (2) The polarization is strongly coupled to oxygen octahedral
rotation (OOR) fluctuations, making its switching inherently difficult; (3) As revealed
by the STEM results, polar domains are highly fragmented into nanoscale regions,
forming a relaxor-ferroelectric-like state that suppresses coordinated long-range
switching.
The observed “leaf-shaped” hysteresis is consistent with a dipole glass state, a
phenomenon reported in a recent study of SrTiO homoepitaxial films, where a similar
3
dipole glass state was induced by local symmetry manipulation (Phys. Rev. Lett. 131,
246801 (2023)). While not constitutive proof on its own, such a characteristic loop
shape has been reported in other emergent ferroelectric systems facing similar
challenges (Nat. Commun. 10, 1409 (2019); Nat. Commun. 16, 6417 (2025)). We
therefore present these data as part of a cumulative body of evidence, while
acknowledging the limitations of the macroscopic measurement.
Secondly, considering the challenges of macroscopic measurement, we turn to
piezoelectric force microscopy (PFM) measurements, providing direct nanoscale
evidence to further illustrate the switching of polarization. As shown in Fig. R4, our
PFM domain switching experiments successfully demonstrate reversible and stable
domain writing and reading. The clear reversal of the PFM phase contrast upon
applying bias pulses of opposite polarities is a definitive proof of ferroelectricity at the
4
micro-scale. This is a widely accepted methodology when P-E loops are inconclusive,
as seen in similar works like room-temperature ferroelectricity in Bi₂O₂Se thin
film (Nano Letters, DOI: 10.1021/acs.nanolett.5c04402) and ferroelectricity in four-
unit-cell freestanding BiFeO
3
